Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

We will continue with module six on corrosion chemistry and today we will discuss the types of electrochemical corrosion, that is differential metal corrosion and differential aeration corrosion.

Key details

  • When we say types of corrosion, we have studied that there are two types.
  • One is dry corrosion and the other one is wet corrosion.
  • Dry corrosion, as we understand, is due to the chemical attack of the environment on the metal surface and it happens in the absence of any conducting medium.
  • But for wet corrosion it has to take place only in conducting medium because what we have is an electrochemical attack.
  • And since most of the times metals are exposed to conducting medium because there's always moisture in the air, therefore wet corrosion is of more importance to us.
  • When we have two.
  • Dissimilar metals in contact with each other and they are exposed to the corrosive environment, that is when we say galvanic corrosion will take place or differential metal corrosion.
  • Two different metals in contact with each other.
  • Therefore, galvanic corrosion can happen very frequently in metals.
  • When we have two different metals.
  • They will have different electrode potentials.
  • The moment they are in contact with each other, one of them which has a greater oxidation tendency becomes the anode, and the one which has lesser oxidation tendency will remain as the cathode.
  • Now, because there will always be in a change in the electrode potentials, this situation or formation of anode and cathode can take place very easily.
  • Now because we are we are talking of electrochemical attack, the most important thing which we should see under any situation is how are this anode and cathode getting formed on the surface and in the presence of the medium conducting medium we will have corrosion happening.
  • Now here because one of the metal has a lower electrode potential or rather.
  • Negative electrode potential that becomes the anode, the other automatically becomes a cathode.
  • And we know that it is only the anode which undergoes oxidation and hence gets corroded, whereas the cathode, the metal which has become cathode, will remain unaffected by carrot.
  • More the difference in the electrode potentials of the two metals.
  • More is going to be the corrosion which will happen, of course, it is only the anode which will corrode.
  • in the presence of oxygen and four electrons giving you four OH minus.
  • We learned that at the cathode there can be different reactions based on the medium.
  • In the atmosphere, and there is moisture.
  • So, therefore, this is the most common reaction which can happen at the cathode.
  • Like we have iron in contact with copper.
  • It is minus 0.44, and copper is 0.34.
  • Copper will become the cathode.
  • The metal will get converted into its ions, therefore the metal is getting destroyed.
  • Whereas at the cathode we know that copper cannot undergo reduction.

Example or application from the lecture

  • Let us understand what is differential metal corrosion.
  • Let us see what will be the reactions.
  • Now we'll consider this most commonly happening because there's always plenty of oxygen.

Core explanation · 05:00–09:59

Unaffected by this type of corrosion when it is in contact with iron.

Key details

  • And what will be the reaction which is happening?
  • Just now we said that oxygen with the H2O plus two electron is giving you 2 OH minus.
  • Earlier it was iron in contact with copper.
  • Therefore, what will happen?
  • Zinc is a more active metal as compared to iron.
  • Therefore, zinc will now act as the anode and the cathode will now be the iron.
  • Iron was undergoing corrosion, whereas when it is in contact with zinc, it is zinc which will undergo corrosion.
  • In the first case, where we had iron in contact with copper, we will get copper hydroxide iron hydroxide.
  • Very common is when we have steel screws or rivets in copper sheets.
  • That it we observe here in this case, in this picture, that it is the steel nut which is getting corroded whereas the bolt remains absolutely intact.
  • And similarly if we have a copper sheet with steel screws, there also we will find that the copper sheet remains in sack intact and it's only the steel screws which will get corroded.
  • And very common again you can see this nice picture which is showing the steel pipe connected to copper plumbing.
  • But what is getting corroded?
  • It is only the steel pipe and not the copper plumbing.
  • this is very commonly seen if you have an iron rod which is lying, you can have a part of it which is exposed to different types of concentration of the oxygen could be different in one area and it could be different in the other area.
  • Which is exposed to lower concentration of oxygen becomes anodic in nature and undergoes corrosion, whereas the other part of the metal which has a higher oxygen concentration becomes cathodic and is unaffected by the.
  • Now, the because of the difference in this oxygen concentration, we are getting something like a oxygen concentration cell on the surface of the metal.
  • And this potential difference will cause the current to a small amount of current corrosion current to flow.
  • We have anode the same metal will undergo corrosion.

Example or application from the lecture

  • Another example, let us take where we have now iron in contact with zinc.
  • So this is a very clear example of galvanic corrosion or differential metal corrosion.
  • Let us see what are the reactions and you can see here.

Core explanation · 10:00–14:59

Oxygen absorption is the reaction we are going to look at.

Key details

  • We have one part which is.
  • Immersed in water or is less oxygenated, and the other part is more oxygenated.
  • It could be water, it could be any other area which is less oxygenated.
  • One part is exposed to less oxygenated, another part is exposed to more oxygenated region so that is exposed to more oxygen.
  • Now because the oxygen absorption takes place at the cathole, so higher concentration of oxygen wherever we have.
  • That area becomes the cathode, whereas the other part where there is less oxygen now becomes the anode, and because it's the anode which undergoes corrosion, that is the metal will take part in this reaction here, whereas here there's a lot of oxygen, so oxygen will be involved.
  • the is always involved at the cathodic region so this area exposed to more oxygen is going to become the cathode whereas the part exposed to less oxygen is going to become the anode.
  • When you pull out a nail from the wall, what do you observe?
  • The part of the nail which is inside the wall, you can see here the part which was inside the wall.
  • The wall has got rusted, whereas the part which was outside did not get rusted.
  • The reason that because this part was exposed to less oxygen, that this acted as the cathode and the part exposed to.
  • Sorry, this part which was exposed to less oxygen became the anode and the part exposed to more oxygen now has become the cathode.
  • We see in this case that the part exposed to.
  • Exposed to less oxygen becomes the anode and the part exposed to more oxygen becomes the cathode.
  • And therefore we see the formation of anode and cathode on the surface of the nail and the part inside the wall which was exposed to less oxygen is getting the same.
  • getting corroded whereas the part exposed to more oxygen is not getting corroded.
  • As you can see in the picture, the part where they are crossing each other, the two wires are crossing each other, you can see that it has got corroded, whereas the part exposed outside it is not getting corroded.
  • The reason again the part which is crossing each other there the amount of oxygen is less and therefore that acts as the anode whereas the part exposed to more oxygen now this other part so.
  • These parts you can see are more corroded.
  • You can see the yellowish orangish color over here, the rust getting formed, whereas the other part look intact.
  • That is acting as the cathode.
  • That part is getting corroded, whereas the part exposed to more oxygen is not getting corroded.
  • What do we see there?
  • The part which is inside the paper has got corroded.
  • All of you would have experienced this.
  • The part which is inside the paper has got corroded, whereas the part which was outside of the paper has not got corroded.
  • Now in tomorrow's class, in the next class, we are going to talk about a special type of differential aeration corrosion.
  • And that is waterline corrosion.
  • And we also go to another type of corrosion that is pitting corrosion.

Example or application from the lecture

  • And let us assume that it's a neutral medium.
  • This is a wonderful example.
  • Another good example would be a wire mesh.
